title: Usage myths and real rules
note: Some school 'rules' are not rules of English. Splitting an infinitive ('to boldly go'), ending a sentence with a preposition, and starting a sentence with And or But are all standard. Real rules, such as subject-verb agreement, describe what careful writers of edited English consistently do.

items.c: Is 'to boldly go' an error?
items.a: no; split infinitives are standard

items.c: Split infinitive
items.a: a word placed between 'to' and its verb

items.c: When a split infinitive is the better choice
items.a: when moving the adverb would be awkward or unclear
items.ex: He wants to really understand it.

items.a: the 19th century

items.c: Is 'What are you looking at?' correct?
items.a: yes; ending with a preposition is fine

items.a: English grammar is not modeled on Latin

items.a: yes; 'because' may open a full sentence

read.title: Rules that never were
text: Many writers carry around rules they learned in school that no serious authority supports. The best known is the ban on splitting infinitives. An infinitive is to plus a verb, and splitting means putting a word between them, as in "to boldly go." English writers have done this since the fourteenth century. Grammarians began to condemn it only in the nineteenth century, and today usage guides accept it, especially when it makes a sentence clearer.

The ban on ending a sentence with a preposition has a similar history. It was promoted in the seventeenth century, most famously by the poet John Dryden, and it reflects a wish to make English behave like Latin. English is not Latin. "What are you looking at?" is natural and correct; "At what are you looking?" is stiff.

None of this means anything goes. Subject-verb agreement, correct pronoun case and clear sentence boundaries are real conventions of edited English, followed by careful writers everywhere. The skill is telling the difference between a rule that describes good practice and a superstition that only makes prose awkward.
